newsitem.title: ITALY: Pope's surgery a success, doctors say no tumour.
newsitem.headline: Pope's surgery a success, doctors say no tumour.

text.p: Pope John Paul had his appendix removed on Tuesday in a "textbook" operation that found no sign of a tumour or other serious illness, the chief surgeon on the medical team said.

Professor Francesco Crucitti told a news conference at Rome's Gemelli hospital that the 76-year-old Pontiff had shown no ill effects from the 50-minute operation and could be back on his feet on Wednesday.
"When he came round he greeted everybody and thanked them. He was calm throughout," Crucitti said.
Calling the operation a "textbook" appendectomy", he said it had not revealed any recurrence of the tumour which Crucitti removed from the Pope's colon in 1992.
"He has never had any other growth (since then). Never," Crucitti said. "There are no secrets...it was exactly what the pre-operative tests showed."

The Vatican's announcement last month that three bouts of fever which have afflicted the Pope since Christmas had been caused by recurrent inflammation of the appendix had met with scepticism from the media and independent doctors.

Some doctors had speculated that the Pope, almost killed by an assassin's bullet in 1981 that led to emergency abdominal surgery, might have another tumour. The one Crucitti removed in 1992 was the size of an orange and starting to turn malignant.

Crucitti said the operation and subsequent routine tissue analysis had "excluded the presence of other pathologies" (problems) but he sidestepped a barrage of questions about a violent trembling of the left hand which troubles the Pope.
The Vatican has not denied reports that the trembling, along with facial rigidity and a stooped gait, could be signs of Parkinson's Disease, a debilitating neurological disorder.
"There are specialists who are following him. This is not my field," Crucitti said.

The Polish-born Pope, who has asked the world's Roman Catholics to pray for him, was taken to the operating theatre early on Tuesday from his 10th floor suite at the Gemelli which has its own chapel where he heard mass.
He spent about two hours in the operating theatre but Crucitti said surgery itself lasted only 50 minutes.

It was conducted by traditional incision rather than modern keyhole surgery because of scar tissue and "adhesions" left from previous abdominal surgery, which Crucitti carried out twice after the 1981 shooting and in 1992.
He said the wound had required about 10 stitches and that doctors had also separated some of the adhesions.
Adhesions, when normally separate tissues stick together, occur between loops of intestine after abdominal surgery.
Crucitti said the Pope could leave his bed for the first time on Wednesday and might be out of hospital in less than seven days.

The "Pilgrim Pope", who will enter his 19th year as leader of the world's Roman Catholics later this month, has repeatedly said he wants to lead the Church into the third millennium and has kept up a punishing schedule despite frailty and fatigue.
While Crucitti and other members of his team pronounced the operation, and pre-surgery tests, a success, the surgeon suggested the Pope might consider slowing down.
"If I could venture my own opinion, I think that the Pope should rest more," Crucitti said.
